profile.reading:
DataBank DFW1 sits at 400 South Akard Street, Dallas, Texas, the former Federal Reserve Building in downtown Dallas' central business district; this record's own OpenStreetMap address tag (400 South Akard Street, Dallas, TX 75202) matches DataBank's published DFW1 address exactly, confirming the identification. DataBank's own facility page and DFW1 datasheet state 145,250 square feet of raised-floor space and 7 megawatts of critical IT load, with 2N critical IT power design, N+1 cooling, roughly 40 to 44 onsite network carriers functioning as a carrier-hotel building, and FISMA/FedRAMP, SOC 1/2, HIPAA, PCI DSS, and ISO 27001:2022 compliance certifications. DataBank cites 100 percent renewable energy sourcing for DFW1 but does not name the power utility on the facility page; Oncor is the incumbent Dallas-Fort Worth transmission and distribution utility as a matter of public record and is named explicitly by DataBank on its Plano and Red Oak campus materials. DataBank does not publish a year-opened date for DFW1 on its current site, though the building's history as a former Federal Reserve facility implies a repurposed structure predating DataBank's own operation of it as a data center. DataBank is headquartered in Dallas and operates roughly ten facilities across the DFW metro totaling 866,640 square feet and 193.8 megawatts of combined critical IT load, making DFW1's downtown carrier-hotel role a flagship anchor of the company's home market alongside its newer suburban Plano and Red Oak campuses.

Downtown Dallas's Akard Street corridor, anchored by DFW1's former Federal Reserve building, sits within the city's historic financial district, a few blocks from the Dallas Area Rapid Transit system's core downtown stations, giving DFW1 unusually direct downtown transit and fiber-route access compared with DataBank's newer suburban Plano and Red Oak facilities. Texas's broader data center boom has prompted ERCOT to substantially revise its long-term electricity demand forecasts upward to account for data center and other large-load growth statewide, a dynamic that has shaped debate in the Texas Legislature over large-load interconnection rules and cost allocation between data centers and other ratepayers.

reading.body:
This facility has no published power specification and cannot be ranked among Texas data centers by capacity. The operator DataBank lists twelve numbered buildings across the Dallas-Fort Worth area, but the address for this particular row could not be confirmed from citable sources and remains unresolved among four candidates in Dallas proper. Without a verified address or published megawatts, this entry does not contribute to the state inventory.

Texas has 133 mapped data center facilities, of which 18 publish power capacity totaling 468 megawatts. This facility's rank as 19th by published megawatts is a classification artifact reflecting the absence of a published figure rather than a measured position in the state's infrastructure.

The entry cannot be read for AI relevance without verified location, power capacity, or connectivity specifications. Any assessment of this campus's role in AI scaling infrastructure in Texas must wait for operator disclosure of these facts.
